title: Why multiply both parts of two thirds by four?
description: A strip cut into three equal parts shows two thirds. Cutting every part into four rows turns thirds into twelfths, the same size of piece three fourths was given, and shows why the multiplier is four. Keeko's doubt is that the multiplier three can be used again.
teaching_notes: One idea: each fraction gets its own multiplier, chosen so that both reach the same bottom number. Four is chosen because three times four is twelve. Watch for the slip of reusing the multiplier three, which gives ninths instead of twelfths.

source: In 2/3 = (2×4)/(3×4) = 8/12, why did we choose to multiply both the numerator and denominator here by 4?
video_script.why: The child sees that each fraction gets its own multiplier, chosen so that both reach the same common bottom number, twelve.
video_script.substitution: The book's strip, with every equal part cut into the same number of rows; the shaded length does not change, only the count of rows.
video_script.anchor: a strip cut into three equal parts with two shaded, as in the book, with three fourths already written as nine twelfths beside it
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko wants to multiply by three again, as was done for three fourths. That cuts the strip into ninths, which still do not match twelfths, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: Both fractions now count in the same unit, one twelfth

final_answer.spoken: multiply by four, so that three becomes twelve

video_script.fraction_reading: two thirds, three fourths, eight twelfths, nine twelfths, six ninths, one twelfth
never_show: Keeko's slip written before the Keeko part
why 3/4 is multiplied by 3 explained again
maths_rules: the strip is one whole cut into 3 equal parts; 2 parts are shaded, which is 2/3
3/4 has already been written in twelfths: 3/4 = 9/12
each part cut into 4 rows: 3 × 4 = 12 rows, and 2 × 4 = 8 shaded rows
multiplying the top and the bottom by 4 keeps the shaded length the same
Keeko's slip: (2 × 3)/(3 × 3) = 6/9 is equal to 2/3 but counts in ninths, not twelfths
video_script.design: One idea: each fraction gets its own multiplier to reach the one common bottom number. The strip stays on the board from start to end.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; the line 3/4 − 2/3; under it 2/3 = (2×4)/(3×4) = 8/12 with both fours circled; the words why four?

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears with 3/4 − 2/3
marks.ask: both fours are circled and the words why four? appear

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about taking away fractions.
<bookmark mark='step'/>Three fourths was written as nine twelfths, and two thirds became eight twelfths.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Why did we multiply the top and the bottom of two thirds by four?

beats.on_screen: the working holds still and the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a strip cut into 3 equal parts with 2 parts shaded and labelled 2/3; beside it the label 3/4 = 9/12

marks.strip: a strip cut into 3 equal parts appears with 2 parts shaded and labelled 2/3
marks.twelfths: the label 3/4 = 9/12 appears beside the strip

narration: <bookmark mark='strip'/>Here is a strip cut into three equal parts, with two parts shaded. That is two thirds.
<bookmark mark='twelfths'/>Beside it, three fourths is already written as nine twelfths.
Two thirds must be written in twelfths too, to match.

marks.given: the two fractions are written on the working board

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, three fourths is already nine twelfths, and two thirds has the bottom number three.

beats.on_screen: To find: why 2/3 is multiplied by 4 on the top and the bottom

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find why the multiplier for two thirds is four.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: the bottom number to reach is 12, the bottom of 9/12

marks.target: the 12 under 9/12 glows and an arrow points to the 3 under 2/3

narration: <bookmark mark='target'/>Step one, find the bottom number we must reach.
Three fourths already counts twelfths, so two thirds must reach twelve too.

marks.ask: 3 × ? = 12 is written with a glowing question mark
marks.four: the question mark becomes 4 and 3 × 4 = 12 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='ask'/>Step two, find what to multiply three by to reach twelve.
<bookmark mark='four'/>Three times four is twelve, so the multiplier is four.

marks.mult: the top 2 and the bottom 3 are each multiplied by 4

narration: <bookmark mark='mult'/>Step three, multiply the top and the bottom by four, so the fraction keeps its size.
<bookmark mark='eight'/>Two times four is eight, and three times four is twelve.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: check on the strip: 3 × 4 = 12 rows, 2 × 4 = 8 shaded rows; the shaded length is unchanged

marks.rows: each of the 3 parts is cut into 4 equal rows and 12 rows appear
marks.shade: 8 shaded rows glow and the shaded length stays the same

narration: <bookmark mark='rows'/>Step four, check on the strip. Cut each of the three parts into four equal rows.
That makes twelve rows.
<bookmark mark='shade'/>Eight of them are shaded, and the shaded length has not changed.

beats.on_screen: Answer: both fractions count the same unit, 1/12; we multiply by 4 because 3 × 4 = 12

marks.ans: 9/12 and 8/12 sit side by side with the label same unit, 1/12

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Both fractions now count in the same unit, one twelfth.
<bookmark mark='why'/>We multiply by four to turn three into twelve, the bottom number three fourths already has.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the strip
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 2/3 = (2×3)/(3×3) = 6/9; a strip cut into 9 parts sits beside the strip cut into 12 parts and the cuts do not line up; the bubble is struck through

marks.doubt: Keeko's bubble shows both numbers multiplied by 3, giving 6/9
marks.ninths: a strip cut into 9 parts appears beside 9/12 and the cuts do not line up
marks.fix: the bubble is struck through and the multiplier 4 returns

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks we multiply by three again, as we did for three fourths.
Two times three is six, and three times three is nine.
<bookmark mark='ninths'/>That gives six ninths, a strip cut into ninths, but three fourths is counted in twelfths.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Ninths and twelfths are different sizes, and we cannot take them away. Each fraction needs its own multiplier.
